content: The test image shows a soybean plant with completely wilted, dried brown leaves that are curled and still attached to the stem. The plant appears to have died rapidly. Let me examine reference images for the top candidates.
The Phytophthora reference (top-left) shows plants with completely wilted/dead leaves still attached to stems - very similar to the test image. Let me check a few more candidates.

The Phytophthora reference (top-left panel) shows plants that have completely died with dried, brown leaves still attached in wet/muddy conditions - matching our test image very closely. Let me check one more comparison.

**Analysis Summary:**

**Test image features:**
- Mid-season soybean plant completely dead/wilted
- Leaves are brown, curled, dried, and still attached to the erect stem
- Very wet/muddy soil conditions visible
- Rapid whole-plant death appearance
- No visible lesion patterns on leaves (just uniform death)

**Candidate comparison:**
- **Phytophthora**: Top-left reference panel shows identical presentation — plants completely killed with brown dried leaves still attached to erect stems, in wet/muddy soil conditions. Symptom description matches: "damping off, stunting, yellowing" and "dark brown lesion on lower stem extending up from taproot, girdles the stem." Wet conditions are classic Phytophthora trigger.
- **Sudden_death_syndrome**: Reference shows yellow/green interveinal chlorosis on leaves — not present here. SDS leaves drop leaflets while petioles remain, which doesn't match the fully intact wilted leaves.
- **Pythium_damping_off**: Affects seedlings with soft rot at soil line — plant here is more developed.
- **Anthracnose**: Shows mature/end-season drying, not the same rapid wilt pattern.
- **Rhizoctonia/Fusarium**: Focus on stem/root lesions, not whole-plant collapse.

The wet soil, erect but completely dead plant with dried leaves still attached, and the close visual match to Phytophthora reference images all support this classification.
